Moscow, which had previously insisted that European representatives had no place at the negotiating table, has now softened its stance.

Moscow has signalled for the first time that it would not oppose a European representatives taking part in negotiations on Ukraine, thereby confirming about the possible participation of an EU delegation in the next round of peace talks.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow had no intention to dictate who should represent the EU at the negotiating table, even though it had previously insisted that EU representatives had "no business" there.

"We cannot and do not want to set conditions for their negotiating team. Shift in Kremlin rhetoric

Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2024, has previously accused Europe of "prolonging the war" and "multiplying the suffering of ordinary people" by supporting Kyiv.

On Tuesday, negotiators from the United States, Ukraine and Russia held trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, which European representatives were excluded from.

A few days later on Thursday, US envoy Jared Kushner announced that Russia had agreed to expand the next round of talks to include European participation.

EU leaders agreed Friday that Europe would be represented by Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the bloc's institutions.

Dozens of Portuguese cities saw protests Saturday against the housing shortage. Demonstrators demand rent caps, stronger tenant protection and more public housing.

Under the slogan "they will not steal our right to live here," thousands gathered for nationwide demonstrations across Portugal on Saturday to protest the rising cost of housing and stagnating incomes.

Demonstrators took to the streets of Lisbon and dozens of other cities calling for limits on rent increases, stronger protection from evictions, more public housing and measures to curb housing speculation.

"We need homes to live in, not homes to speculate on. Public housing needs to be built and the price of rents needs to come down," Raquel Ferreira from the housing-rights movement 'Casa Para Viver' told local media at the start of the demonstration in Porto.

The protests come as the government adopted a new bill that would make it easier and faster for property owners to evict tenants.

"What should happen, and what this massive mobilisation across the country is demanding, is the withdrawal of this draft law," said José Manuel Pureza, coordinator of the Left Bloc.

The new housing bill includes measures that could further exacerbate the housing crisis

The proposed legislation seeks to make it easier for landlords to regain possession of rented properties by speeding up the procedure for property-owners to evict tenants.

It would also give landlords greater freedom to set rental prices by removing rent caps, allow them to demand higher upfront payments such as deposits and advance rent, and changes the rules regarding older rental contracts signed before 1990.

The government argues that these measures will encourage landlords to put more properties on the rental market. However, Casa para Viver believes it will leave tenants more vulnerable and instead calls for rent regulation to ensure housing costs are regulated in relation to people's incomes.

Casa para Viver criticised the government for viewing €2,300 as a "moderate" income, when "more than half the people working in this country earn less than 1,000 euros."

Properties worth up to €660,000 are now also classified as having "moderate" value on the property market.

"The government and the parties that have allowed these measures to pass are pushing prices up and normalising the absurd, while rewarding landlords, developers and property funds," the organisation wrote in March.

Portugal records the third largest rise in housing costs in Europe

Housing prices relative to incomes across Portugal rose 60.8% between 2015 and 2025, according to EU data, well ahead of the Netherlands in second place in the EU at 34.3%.

The highest spikes were recorded in Lisbon and Porto.

Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, house prices rose by almost 20%, the National Statistics Institute (INE) reported at the end of October.

Rents have also risen sharply, with an increase of 68% since 2020, according to the government.

Speaking to Euronews Business, economist Mike Langen said thatPortugal "experienced a tourism boom, and their golden visa program attracted foreign investors, so house prices grew partly because of foreign capital".

Foreign buyers and investment funds drove up prices by buying Portuguese property, including buildings in poor condition.

Casa Para Viver is now calling on the government to adopt measures to tackle property speculation, and demands for an end to golden visas and to incentives for digital nomads, as well as an end to tax exemptions for property funds.

The country’s pleasant climate and long coastline have helped make it popular among digital nomads and other remote workers, as well as retirees from abroad.

Tourism has also risen sharply, with many city-centre flats being turned into short-term rentals and subsequently taken out of the long-term rental market.

Portuguese people excluded from the property market

The average salary in Portugal is around €2,200 a month, according to official statistics.

A one-bedroom apartment in the centre of Lisbon typically costs at least €1,100, according to property agents.

For many households, a single income is no longer enough to cover the rent on a family-sized flat in the centre of a large city.

According to a report published by the Deutsche Bank Research Institute (DBRI), disposable income is what remains of a household's net monthly salary after rent has been paid.Across the 28 European cities analysed, disposable income after rent ranges from €253 in Lisbon to €9,140 in Zurich.

The report also reveales that Lisbon and Milan are the most challenging cities to live in for couples.

Lisbon residents say they are being excluded from the property market because of high prices. On average, Lisbon households are left with only €253 to live on for the month after paying the rent. Net pay in Lisbon is €1,408, but the rent can reach €2,561 per month, the DBRI concludes.

Young people say they cannot get onto the property ladder, while parents worry that their children have to move far away to find a home. At the same time, some Portuguese homeowners have made substantial profits from selling their properties.

The government is trying to address this crisis with measures such as cutting taxes on new builds, restricting short-term rentals and promising to build 145,000 new homes, although it acknowledges that the effects will not be immediate.

Yellow vests, students, and education unions took to the streets to voice a range of frustrations, from rising cost of living and calls for better funding for education to stronger protection for children and teenagers and a new police law.

Thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Saturday, marking the fifth Saturday of nationwide protests in a row.

The Yellow Vest movement, students, and education unions took to the streets to voice a range of frustrations, from rising cost of living and calls for better funding for education, to stronger protection for children and teenagers and a new police bill.

In Paris, many gathered on the Place de la Republique, which has been a symbolic and common gathering ground for nationwide protests.

"We’re asking to have teachers when we go to class. We’re asking to not have ceilings collapsing on us when we eat in the canteen. We’re asking, when we get our A-levels, despite conditions getting worse every year, to be able to carry on our studies at university," Marius Mesnil, Co-Secretary-General of the Union Syndicale Lycéenne said.

France has been rocked by school blockades and protests for more than a month.

The interior ministry estimated around 106,000 people took to the streets nationwide on Saturday, including 24,000 in Paris. Organisers put this number at 200,000, including 100,000 in the capital.

The turnout of Saturday's protest was lower than usual. The largest protest in recent weeks took place on Thursday, during a union-led strike. More than half a million people took to the streets across the country.

The unions have called for another day of strike action next Tuesday, after rejecting the government's promise to raise the minimum wage by 0.6%, which they say is not enough.

"The government has only given us crumbs, and we want the whole bakery," Benjamin Ball, a member of the Yellow Vest movement said.

'License to kill' bill

Demonstrators also expressed opposition to a new police bill that would grant police officers and gendarmes additional protection when using firearms in line of duty.

Supporters of the bill—including Marine Le Pen's far-right party, currently the favourite in opinion polls in the presidential race—argue that the new law is needed to prevent law enforcement officers being automatically presumed guilty of using excessive force.

However, unions say the bill amounts to a "license to kill" for police, and would make it even more difficult to hold law enforcement officials accountable. In France, cases of alleged police brutality rare reach a criminal court.

"What the so‑called 'licence to kill' law, which is being put to the vote next week, provides for is literally that a police officer who fires will first be presumed to have acted lawfully," Sabrine Kharbach, spokesperson for the Student Union said.

"Yet another layer of impunity for those who club us, gas us and maim us. Yet another layer of impunity for this police force that acts as the armed wing of the state," she added.

Kenza, 28, was among the thousands of demonstrators taking to the streets in the city of Toulouse, in southern France. "The repression of protesters is unacceptable, especially when children are involved".

Last week, lawyers representing at least 18 people injured during protests in France in recent weeks said they would sue the interior ministry over his responsibility for alleged police brutality, local media reported.

They condemned the use of force by police at the demonstrations, which they said had resulted in "mutilations," including injuries to protesters' hands, feet and eyes.

Canada has concluded talks with the Philippines on a free trade deal, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on Saturday, as Ottawa continues to look to reduce its reliance on the US following a breakdown in relations with Washington.

"One year ago, Canada and the Philippines launched talks on a new free trade agreement," Carney wrote in a post on social media. "Today, we’ve already concluded the negotiations."

"We’re diversifying our trade partnerships to build a stronger, more resilient Canadian economy," Carney, who is in Manila to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit, added.

Speaking to the media on the sidelines of the summit, Carney said his government would work quickly to finalise the deal and that it would come into force in 2027. It is expected to take around six months for the agreement to be signed, he added.

"This is good news for Canadians in the agriculture sector, in the aerospace sector, even in AI, and our businesses working across forest products, mining, energy, services and beyond," he told reporters.

Ottawa is also hoping to secure a broader trade deal with the 11-member ASEAN group as a whole. Negotiations on such an arrangement have been "substantially completed," per Carney.

The prime minister said Saturday's announcements were "part of a strategy of developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities for our businesses, more choice for Canadians, better jobs for our workers and reducing our relative reliance on the United States."

Canada has been seeking to double non-US exports by 2035 and has been aligning itself more closely with Europe as part of its push to reduce its reliance on the US, prompted by repeated clashes with US President Donald Trump over trade.

Trump is due to arrive in Manila early next week, before heading on to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen. Carney is scheduled to next head to Cambodia before also arriving in China.

A fast-moving reshape of the Gulf and Middle East multilateral security landscape is underway, triggered by the Iran war and the US signals that it is adapting its long-standing security presence in the region.

Turkey and Qatar signed a landmark mutual defence agreement on Friday, strengthening their strategic and security partnership for deterrence amid a rapidly changing security landscape of the Gulf and the Middle East.

Turkish president President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met in Istanbul on Friday to co-chair the Supreme Strategic Committee between Qatar and Turkey, concluding a wide range of bilateral agreements.

The two leaders adopted the mutual defence agreement "aimed at bolstering collective defence and achieving regional security and stability, as well as adopting a unified position in the face of any external armed attack targeting either or both parties", according to a joint statement released by the two countries.

"The two parties agreed to hold consultations on threats to their security... and to strengthen cooperation through joint military exercises, collaboration in the field of defence industries, and the exchange of personnel training," the statement said.

Both countries said that their agreement underlines their shared vision of a more secure and stable regional order, with Erdogan’s office stating that it will “add a new dimension to the brotherly ties between the two countries."

"President Erdogan stated that ​we would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in the ​Gulf region and establish a basis for dialogue and achieve peace," according to a Turkish presidency statement on X, and that the agreement will expand defence industry cooperation between the two countries.

Turkey and Qatar would continue working together "to prevent a renewed outbreak of war in the Gulf region and to promote dialogue and peace", Erdogan said.

The leaders discussed Israel's attacks on Gaza and the humanitarian situation in the Palestinian territory, efforts towards normalisation in Syria and the latest developments in Libya, the statement added.

Qatar and Turkey also signed multiple agreements on trade and energy cooperation as well as diplomacy, education and culture.

A new map of regional defensive alliances is taking shape

The new partnership comes at a time of rapid regional defence realignments triggered by the Iran war as Turkey, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Indonesia have been shaping a new map of defence alliances in the region in a matter of a few months.

The Gulf nations have been clear that the United States' regional security umbrella continues to be central to their security architecture, but with Washington signalling its own global realignment, the Gulf countries are now widening their defence strategies, in the context of the ongoing "no war, no peace" reality.

In August, Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement,” a regional defence pact under which the three countries would come to each other's aid if one of them came under attack.

Ratified by the Turkish parliament last week, the pact links NATO member Turkey, which has the alliance's second-largest military, with Pakistan, the Muslim world's only nuclear-armed state, and Saudi Arabia, the Gulf's leading power.

Turkey has said the agreement is not aimed at any other country and remains open to other states, including Egypt.

Also in August, Pakistan and Kuwait signed a joint defence and military cooperation agreement.

In October, Qatar, Turkey, Pakistan and Indonesia signed the “Badr” multilateral memorandum of understanding on defence industry cooperation.

The Bundeswehr is moving into retail: with its own online shop, the German armed forces aim to improve their public image and establish themselves as a brand. The launch range includes T-shirts, mugs and a rubber duck armed with an assault rifle – which proved so popular that it quickly sold out.

Anyone who likes a bit of military company in the bath might soon find just what they are looking for at the Bundeswehr. Germany's armed forces have launched their own online shop, and one of its most eye-catching products is, of all things, a camouflage-clad rubber duck armed with a miniature assault rifle.

What might initially sound like a joke is, in fact, part of a new marketing strategy. Through the shop, the Bundeswehr aims to reshape its public image, raise its profile and, above all, appeal to younger audiences. Alongside the unusual rubber duck, the range also features other branded merchandise and clothing.

Bundeswehr duck makes a splash

The duck is attracting particular attention. The small rubber toy, dressed in military gear, has quickly become a bestseller and was temporarily sold out shortly after the shop launched.

Demand for the new online shop has exceeded expectations, reportedly causing technical issues soon after launch. Clearly, military-themed marketing can make quite a splash, even when it ends up in the bath.

Bundeswehr seeks to boost its public image

Behind the unusual merchandise is a serious objective: the Bundeswehr wants to raise its public profile and build its brand beyond barracks, trade fairs and recruitment campaigns.

Recruitment is a key priority as the armed forces seek to expand their ranks. The merchandise is designed to make the Bundeswehr more visible in everyday life and strengthen its connection with the public.

Criticism of military marketing

Not everyone is convinced by the new strategy. Critics warn that merchandise and light-hearted promotional items risk trivialising the realities of military service. The marketing of weapons and military equipment as lifestyle products has drawn particular criticism.

The strategy has also drawn criticism from politicians. Representatives of the Left Party warn that such marketing risks making the military an increasingly normal part of everyday life.

From the parade ground to the bathtub

Whether the rubber duck will actually help attract new recruits remains to be seen. But as a promotional tool, it has already completed its first mission: generating attention, sparking conversation and, apparently, selling out in record time.

And who knows what might come next? Perhaps a lifebuoy in Bundeswehr camouflage for emergencies in the bubble bath, or a mini drone to keep an eye on rising foam levels.

A camp bed for exhausted bath ducks could also be on the cards. After all, the troops need to be prepared for every mission – even in the bubble bath.

The huge crowds turning out to see the 71-year-old pontiff have prompted heightened fears among health authorities in Latin America, which has seen a surge in measles cases this year.

Pope Leo XIV is holding a mass in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba in northern Peru on Saturday as he continues his tour of South America, drawing huge crowds as people seek to catch a glimpse of the 71-year-old pontiff.

After travelling by helicopter from Chiclayo air base to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, Leo flies back for a prayer meeting with the Catholic community at the shrine of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo in the evening.

The pope returned to his beloved former hometown of Chiclayo on Friday.

The Chicago-born pontiff, who previously worked as a missionary and then bishop in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship, presided over an open-air mass for around 500,000 people in the city.

"What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!" Leo said. "Thank you for your affection, support and prayers, especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming."

But the huge crowds turning out to see the pope have prompted heightened fears among health authorities in Latin America, which has seen a surge in measles cases this year.

From January to the end of October, 57,666 confirmed cases were recorded in 17 countries and territories in the Americas, almost five times more than in the same period the previous year. At least 81 deaths have been reported.

Ahead of Leo's visit, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) considered the public health risk of measles "very high" in the context of the expected religious mass gatherings.

The concern is mainly linked to low vaccination rates in some countries, particularly Argentina and Peru.

"We’re seeing children not going to school, children being hospitalized," Daniel Salas Peraza, the head of immunization at PAHO, said. "It’s a very complex situation."

Measles

Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease caused by a virus. It can lead to severe complications and is potentially fatal.

The disease infects the respiratory tract and then spreads throughout the body. It can cause symptoms including a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and a rash.

An effective and relatively cheap vaccine is available.

According to the World Health Organisation, "children should receive two doses of the vaccine to ensure they are immune."

"The first dose is usually given at nine months of age in countries where measles is common and 12–15 months in other countries. A second dose should be given later in childhood, usually at 15–18 months," the agency says.

To stop the disease from spreading in a community and to protect infants and others who are unable to get the vaccine, at least 95% of the population must be fully vaccinated.

According to WHO data for 2025, only Uruguay had reached this threshold. In Peru, coverage stood at 90% for the first dose and 82% for the second. In Argentina, the figures fell to 84% and 55% respectively.

Peru has recorded almost 3,000 cases in 2026, the fourth highest number in the Americas after Guatemala, Mexico and the United States.

In the five cities included in the Pope's itinerary - Lima, Chiclayo, Cajamarca, Cusco and Pucallpa - 170 infections have been detected so far this year.

In the run-up to the visit, Peruvian authorities stepped up vaccination campaigns, focusing especially on areas with higher transmission rates.

Initiatives have also included bringing forward vaccination for children between six and eleven months of age and campaigns targeting people up to 29 years old. By the end of September, 1.2 million doses had been administered since the push began in April, while more than two million additional doses were available.

The situation is also tricky in Argentina, where at the end of October, authorities issued a warning about the health risks linked to the Pope's visit. Up to four million people were expected in Buenos Aires province.

Experts are also worried about government cuts to health spending, which have scaled back the structures responsible for planning, funding and monitoring immunisation campaigns.

For its part, Uruguay has launched a period of enhanced epidemiological surveillance across the nation, which will continue until 29 November, weeks after the pope's departure.

Authorities have also intensified appeals to the public to complete their vaccination courses. The aim is to detect any new infections quickly and limit the spread of the virus after the large gatherings.

Investigators uncovered large amounts of cash hidden in a variety of spots: buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings and warehouses, stashed inside residential properties and stored in a high-value safe in a remote location.

Hungarian authorities said they seized more than €17.5 million in cash buried in forests and hidden in other places across the country this week.

On 12 and 13 November, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) carried out coordinated searches at multiple locations across Hungary, including in Budapest and the counties of Pest, Békés and Nógrád, as part of a criminal investigation involving Miklós Seszták, a former minister of national development.

During the searches, investigators uncovered large amounts of cash hidden in a variety of spots: buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings and warehouses, stashed inside residential properties and stored in a high-value safe in a remote location.

Over the course of the two-day operation, investigators recovered a total of 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100. On Friday, NVVH staff paid the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury.

According to the investigation, there is reason to suspect that between 2015 and 2018, Seszták and the CEO of Hungarian National Asset Management (MNV) received more than 11 billion forints in illicit payments from representatives of companies contracted by Volánbusz, a national bus operator.

The NVVH previously announced that an earlier search carried out in October at the Kisvárda home of Seszták had uncovered safes of a type more commonly used by financial service providers and pawnshops.

On 30 September, the Buda Central District Court ordered the detention of Seszták at the request of the NVVH.

In late October, the court announced that Seszták's detention had been extended until 30 January. It cited the seriousness of the case and the risk that he might flee or go into hiding.

The research team used a small electronic capsule that participants swallowed to monitor changes as it passed through the digestive system.

A scientific study carried out by the University of Copenhagen has found that drinking coffee regularly may affect the functioning of the digestive system, especially bowel movements and colon contractions and is also linked to greater diversity of gut bacteria.

The study was published in the journal "Gut Microbiology", which specialises in research on gut microorganisms, and aimed to explore the relationship between habitual coffee consumption and the physiological conditions inside the digestive system.

What does coffee do inside your digestive system?

The research team used a small electronic capsule that participants swallowed to track the changes that occurred as it travelled through the digestive system.

The capsule measured a set of indicators, including the time it took contents to pass through the gastrointestinal tract, temperature, acidity levels and intestinal contractions.

The study involved 61 healthy adults in Denmark, whom the researchers divided into two groups according to how much coffee they consumed.

The first group consisted of people who drank between one and five cups of coffee a day on more than three of the eight days covered by the study, while the second group comprised people who drank coffee less frequently.

The results showed that people who consume coffee regularly have greater diversity in the microorganisms present in their intestines compared with participants who drink less coffee.

This finding is consistent with research suggesting that coffee may influence the composition of the gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microorganisms that live inside the digestive system.

Francesca Bucci, the lead researcher in the study and a PhD student in the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, said that regular coffee consumption seems to affect the physiology of the intestines.

One of the most notable results was that people who drink coffee regularly had much lower acidity levels in the small intestine than those who consume it less often.

The researchers also observed a link between higher coffee intake and a greater number of contractions in the colon, muscle movements that help push intestinal contents through the digestive system.

These contractions play a role in digestion and in keeping bowel movements regular, as they help move waste along and may help prevent constipation and keep the intestinal muscles in good condition.

Bucci said that intestinal contractions can support proper digestion, help reduce constipation and help maintain the functional state of the intestinal muscles.

By contrast, the researchers are still unable to determine whether the lower level of acidity in the small intestine benefits health or could have negative effects.

Is coffee responsible for the changes?

The researchers stress that the study cannot prove that coffee consumption is the direct cause of the changes observed in the digestive system.

However, Henrik Munch Roager, associate professor and head of the research group in the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, believes there are reasons to support the possibility that coffee plays a role in these changes.

He explained that previous studies have shown that coffee affects a range of processes that take place inside the digestive system, including the secretion of acids in the stomach.

He added that this evidence makes it likely that the differences the researchers observed are linked to the effects of coffee rather than being mere coincidence.

He pointed out that many people notice, based on their daily experience, that coffee affects their digestion.

The research team sees the next step as conducting a study that allows control over the amount of coffee participants drink, instead of merely observing their consumption habits and comparing the differences between them.

This type of study would help determine whether coffee is actually causing these changes and to understand the mechanisms through which it may affect bowel movements and contractions.

Canadian authorities said Russians will be barred from the 10-nation tournament in Alberta from 26 December. Estonia, Finland and Norway plan to exclude athletes until the war in Ukraine ends.

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation is insisting that the World Junior Championship, due to take place in Canada next month, be postponed or cancelled after Ottawa decided not to allow the Russian team to take part in the tournament.

As the official Russian news agency TASS reported on Thursday, the president of the Russian Ice Hockey Federation, Vladislav Tretiak, threatened to demand compensation from Canada and possibly also from Germany, which will host the men’s World Championship in 2027, if Russia is barred from participation.

Speaking at a meeting of the Presidential Council for the Development of Physical Culture and Sport in Moscow, Tretiak said he had also appealed to the International Ice Hockey Federation’s (IIHF) ethics committee to open an investigation and impose sanctions on national federations that are organising boycotts of games involving Russia.

"There are rules: if a team does not take to the ice, it suffers a technical defeat and sanctions are imposed," TASS quoted Tretiak as saying. "The IIHF has a way out - either they let us play, or, if we are unable to enter Canada, they move the championship, do not stage it at all, or impose sanctions on the Canadian ice hockey association."

"You cannot bomb Ukrainian cities and then send your juniors... as if you were civilised people"

Tretiak’s statement came a day after Canada confirmed that Russian players would not be allowed to compete in the 10-nation tournament, which is due to begin on 26 December in the province of Alberta. Canada adopted this stance in response to a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) last month that restored Russia’s right to take part in international ice hockey competitions.

That decision overturned the ban the IIHF had imposed on Russia after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"You cannot bomb Ukrainian cities and then send your juniors to Alberta to play hockey, as if you were civilised people. No Russian or Belarusian teams at the World Junior Championship. Not under your flags. Not under any other flags. Period," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an unequivocal statement.

As the Russian sports daily Sport-Express reported (source in Russian), Russia had from the outset expected that visas for the World Championship would be refused, so the Russian Ice Hockey Federation was planning to put together a squad made up solely of players from North American NHL clubs. However, Ottawa said that even these Russians would not be able to play for the national team in any case because their work visas do not allow it.

In addition, Germany and several other countries have refused to sign the new schedule for the World Junior Championship if Russia is included. The head of the German Ice Hockey Association, Frank Lutz, said this at a meeting of the Bundestag’s sports committee (link in German) (source in Russian).

The next tournament in the ice hockey calendar is the women’s under-18 World Championship in Ostrava, Czechia, from 8 to 16 January 2027, but Prague has also made it clear in advance that it will not issue visas to Russian players.

For its part, Germany is considering dropping the men’s World Championship in spring 2027 against the background of a wave of boycotts. Several of the world’s leading ice hockey nations have said they will not play Russia after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled that Russia and Belarus should be readmitted to international ice hockey competitions.

Meanwhile, Germany’s "fringe" parties, the far-right Alternative for Germany and the far-left Die Linke, have called (source in Russian) (link in German) on Berlin not to obstruct the participation of the Russian team.

The International Ice Hockey Federation is so far refraining from commenting on the dispute, finding itself at the centre of a rapidly escalating conflict. A number of national federations, including those of Canada, Sweden, Finland, Germany, Czechia and Latvia, have already announced that they will not play matches against Russia. Some tournament sponsors have also threatened to end their cooperation if Russia is allowed to take part.

For the IIHF, moving the World Junior Championship at such a late stage would be extremely difficult; it would also be very hard to find another country willing to take over as host from Canada. On Sunday Norway said it had received notification from the IIHF that it was being excluded from the tournament, to make room for Russia. The federation itself has not yet announced this change.

Several northern countries plan to bar all Russian athletes

Finland is tightening (source in Russian) (link in English) restrictions on the entry of Russian citizens into the country. On 12 November 2026 the government adopted a decree stating that the entry of Russian citizens poses a threat to Finland’s international relations. The new restrictions cover short-term work carried out on the basis of a visa, including professional sport.

"As long as Russia’s aggressive war continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland. Their entry into the country would pose a threat to Finland’s international relations. The same applies to other types of short-term work on visas that do not serve Finland’s vital national interests," said Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen.

The restrictions will apply to all Russian athletes, including those competing under neutral status. The Foreign Ministry said Russia "uses sport as a propaganda tool and seeks to exploit it to advance the aims of its illegal war of aggression".

Oslo has announced similar steps following Helsinki’s decision. The Norwegian government intends to expel Russian and Belarusian professional athletes and their entourages if they try to enter the country to take part in sporting events while the war in Ukraine continues.

The Norwegian government statement stresses that Russian elite sport is closely linked to the authorities and therefore cannot be "considered in isolation" from the war in Ukraine. Belarus, it notes, has supported and facilitated Russia’s war, according to the text (link in Norwegian) (source in Russian).

"Since Russia continues its brutal war of aggression, the government does not want Russian and Belarusian professional athletes and their support staff to come to Norway to take part in international sporting events," said Minister of Culture and Equality Lubna Boby Jaffery.

The government decision, which will come into force "in the near future", could affect the participation of Moscow and Minsk in several events, in particular the opening round of the FIS Ski Jumping World Cup in Lillehammer from 20 to 22 November.

Finally, the authorities in Tallinn have notified the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) that athletes from Russia and Belarus will not be able to take part in competitions held in Estonia. From 18 to 24 January, Otepää will host the World Championships for juniors and under-23 athletes in Nordic skiing, and in February the World Biathlon Championships will take place at the Tehvandi Sports Centre ski stadium.

"Estonia has firmly condemned Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine from the very beginning. Since then, the Estonian government, the Ministry of Culture and the Estonian Olympic Committee have held to a common position that Russian and Belarusian athletes and teams must not take part in international sports competitions until the war in Ukraine is over," says a letter from the Ministry of Culture to FIS, the details of which have been reported (source in Russian) in the press.

At the same time, there were reports that Russia has refused (source in Russian) to take part in the European Boxing Championships for athletes aged 19 to 22, which will be held from 15 to 24 November in Porec, Croatia. The reasons were the Croatian authorities’ requirement that they compete without the Russian flag and anthem, and the refusal to issue visas to members of the Russian delegation.
